net-01-addressing.title: Addressing and subnetting
net-01-addressing.summary: Two hosts, one switch, and the arithmetic that decides whether they can talk.
net-01-addressing.brief:
## Open the Studio

The **Network Simulator** tool opens the studio in place. Build as you read.

## The topology

Two PCs and a switch. Give the PCs `192.168.10.10/24` and `192.168.10.11/24`,
ping one from the other, and watch the ARP exchange in the packet trace.

## Then break it on purpose

Change one host's mask to `/25`. Ping again.

`192.168.10.10/25` has the range `192.168.10.0` - `192.168.10.127`, and
`192.168.10.11/24` has `192.168.10.0` - `192.168.10.255`. The first host still
believes the second is local; the second one's replies are fine. Now move the
second host to `192.168.10.200/24` and ping from the `/25` host: it thinks the
destination is off-net and looks for a gateway that does not exist.

**A mask mismatch is not symmetrical**, and that is why it is such a confusing
fault to diagnose from one end.

## The arithmetic worth doing by hand

For `10.20.30.45/26`:

- block size = 256 - 192 = 64
- networks: .0, .64, .128, .192
- this address is in .0 - .63
- network `10.20.30.0`, broadcast `10.20.30.63`, hosts .1 - .62

Do three of those on paper before you use a calculator. The pattern is the whole
of subnetting.

docker-01-first.title: Images and your first container
docker-01-first.summary: pull, images, run, ps - and the difference between an image and a container.
docker-01-first.brief:
## An image is a template; a container is a running copy

One image, many containers. The image is read-only; each container gets its own
writable layer on top, which is why two containers from `nginx` cannot see each
other's files.

```
docker version
docker pull nginx
docker images
docker run -d --name web nginx
docker ps
docker ps -a
```

`-d` detaches - the container runs in the background and you get its id back.
Without it you are attached to its output and the terminal blocks.

## ps vs ps -a

`docker ps` shows **running** containers. `docker ps -a` shows every container
that exists, including the exited ones - and a container that exited is still
there, holding its name, until you `docker rm` it. "The name is already in use"
on a container you cannot see is always this.

Try:

```
docker run --name hello hello-world
docker ps
docker ps -a
```

The first shows nothing. The second shows `hello` as `Exited (0)`.

> The **Dashboard** tab reads the same engine. Run a command and watch it appear.
